title: The farmer Guru
hookLine: Guru Nanak spent his last years farming at Kartarpur with his community (Sikh tradition)
carry: a householder's life, lived with God in mind

cards: Visitors came to Kartarpur looking for a holy man, and Sikh tradition says they found a farmer. The fields lay in the Punjab, and the man walking the furrow was a teacher people had traveled to hear.
Tradition says that after years on the road, Guru Nanak, whose teaching began the Sikh path, settled at Kartarpur, a village tradition says he founded himself. And there he farmed.
Those visitors found him working in the fields, then singing with everyone in the evening, then eating at the same shared meal.

teach.h: SONG, FIELDS, SONG, A SHARED MEAL.
teach.b: First, the shape of a day at Kartarpur, as tradition tells it. Hymns of praise in the early morning. Work in the fields through the day.
Hymns again in the evening. And a shared kitchen where everyone ate together, whoever they were. Work and worship weren't two lives.
They were one day. Second, the teaching behind it.
Sikh teaching sums up the Guru's way in short phrases: naam japna, remembering God's name; vand chhakna, sharing what you have; and kirat karni, earning an honest living by your own work.
The Guru Granth Sahib puts it in a line, in paraphrase: the one who eats what they earn by their own labor, and gives some of it away, knows the path. Third, the kind of life it pointed to.
In the Guru's world, some seekers left their families and lived on what others gave them.
Guru Nanak, as Sikhs remember him, taught his followers another way: stay in the world, marry, raise a family, work, share.
Sikh teaching still holds up this ideal. Fourth, a story Sikhs tell from those fields.
A seeker named Lehna came to Kartarpur and served the Guru.
Tradition says that one day, in his good clothes, he carried a heavy bundle of wet grass from the fields on his head, and the mud ran down. He didn't mind. Lehna became the next Guru, Guru Angad.
The Sikh line of Gurus, tradition says, passed on in a farmyard, not a throne room.

how: Sikhs speak of kirat karni, earning an honest living, alongside remembering God and sharing; at gurdwaras, volunteers cook, serve and clean the langar, the shared community kitchen.

o: a vow of silence kept while doing your chores
earning an honest living by your own work
giving away everything to live on alms

games.q: you're a seeker who's traveled to Kartarpur to find a holy man. where do you find Guru Nanak, as tradition tells it?
o: in the fields, farming, then singing with everyone.
games.why: Sikh tradition says he farmed by day, with hymns morning and evening and a shared meal for all.

practice: Bring to mind the people you live or work with, and one ordinary chore you could share with one of them, not for them but with them: cooking, cleaning up, weeding a patch of ground, two pairs of hands on one job.
Breathe in that picture, and breathe out any idea that the chore is beneath you. If you pray, you can remember God's name in your own tradition's way while you sit.

wordCard.voice: Kirat karni. Earning an honest living by your own work, one of the three pillars Guru Nanak taught at Kartarpur. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi in Gurmukhi script, from the Sikh tradition: earning an honest living by your own work.

carryVoice: Your line: a householder's life, lived with God in mind. Work and worship, one day. That's day eight hundred ninety-four.
